newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain rate cuts seen unhindered by U.S. Fed hike.
newsitem.headline: Spain rate cuts seen unhindered by U.S. Fed hike.

text.p: The U.S. interest rate hike should not impede further cuts in Spain's key money market rate in the short term, analysts said on Wednesday.
"I think the Bank of Spain will continue cutting. What will give Spain room will be inflation," said Juan Antonio Mielgo, economist at Bank of America in Madrid.

The Federal Reserve on Tuesday raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent in a bid to keep inflation in check and prolong economic expansion. It was the first U.S. rate rise in two years.
Nevertheless analysts said Spanish monetary policy-makers cannot ignore the eventual impact U.S. interest rates will have on other European countries.

"The rise in U.S. rates is negative (for Spain) in that it will have a direct influence on Germany and consequently on peripheral markets," said Carmen Hernansanz, economist at Merrill Lynch in Madrid.
Some analysts saw the U.S. move, together with signs of increasing growth in the German economy, putting a cap on further Bundesbank cuts in the repo rate.
"The possibility of Germany lowering the repo was small and now it is nil. Something similar could happen in France," Hernansanz added.

Though analysts said they expect Spanish inflation to continue improving until May, the risk of a pick-up after that and forecasts of an acceleration in economic growth could put a brake on monetary easing in the second half of the year.
"Inflation will fall until May but after it could pick up. If the economy continues to show signs of growth...I don't think the Bank of Spain is going to remain passive," Mielgo said.
The Spanish government has forecast Gross Domestic Product growth at 3.0 percent for 1997 but Mielgo said he thinks that estimate may be too optimistic.
Analysts at home and abroad say Spain should have room to manoeuvre on interest rates in the medium term, provided U.S. rates do not rise too quickly.
But this may not prove to be the case.
"I don't think this (U.S. rate) hike is going to be the last before the end of the year," said Hernansanz.
Some analysts wondered whether the Fed would continue to act preemptively to stem potential inflation. To determine this, they said the next round of U.S. macroeconomic data will be key.
